maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Would the minister inform the house of the results of his talks with United States officials concerning energy resources and, in particular, whether the U.S. officials have expressed concern at the size of Canadian gas and oil shipments to that country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday I visited Washington as part of a regular program of visits to our principal trading partners. During the course of the visit I met with various officials of the United States government, including Secretary Harriman, Secretary Udall, under secretary George Ball, assistant secretaries Kelly and Johnson and
other officials of the state and interior departments. We discussed mutual problems of trade and development consequent upon the recent GATT discussions at Geneva, where we supported the United States initiative toward trade liberalization. We also discussed matters pertaining to energy in all its forms, on a basis of mutual interest and development. I should make it clear, however, that our discussions did not include any conversations concerning the Columbia river treaty.
I proposed to the Americans that our two countries initiate and undertake joint studies concerning the development of all forms of energy-oil, natural gas, coal, electricity and nuclear power-in which our interests increasingly intertwine. I found our American friends interested in and receptive to the suggestion, and I hope that preliminary discussions will begin in the near future.
As to oil, we also discussed the prospective growth of Canadian exports in the light of United States import control policy. I am sure all hon. members are aware that from time to time since the national oil policy came into effect, American officials have expressed concern about a too rapid rate of growth of our exports of oil to the United States. They reiterated this concern at our meeting on Monday.
The discussions were conducted in a friendly atmosphere and I believe that the outcome will be mutually satisfactory.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact that the minister made this statement on orders of the day limits the ability of the opposition to make any comments on it. Therefore I will have to use the technique of asking a question or two, if I may, to clarify the statement he just made.
My first question is this. In this discussion with the United States were gas imports from Canada to the United States considered in their relationship to oil imports?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I said in my statement, we discussed the whole field of energy, which included gas, of course. It related to oil, nuclear energy and the whole field of energy.

speechtext:

maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S.
speechtext: We did not discuss that problem specifically, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANADIAN AGREEMENT TO FARE INCREASES ON ATLANTIC ROUTE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Transport a question. In view of the reported dissatisfaction of the Canadian air authority with the increases in air fares on the Atlantic route, can the minister tell us why our authority agreed to or negotiated such an increase as was announced last night?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: CANADIAN AGREEMENT TO FARE INCREASES ON ATLANTIC ROUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the authority did not negotiate such an increase. What happened was that last fall the international air line companies had a meeting in Arizona, where an agreement was made to increase fares. Our air transport authority did not agree to those fare increases. There were further meetings as a consequence of the failure of the air transport board, the Canadian government air authority, and the United States authorities to agree to the increases.
This further conference of the air line companies took place in Bermuda and was continued in Montreal last Friday, when a compromise was reached. I hope to put the details of the compromise on record in a moment, and it goes into operation on June 1. These new compromise fares were approved by the air transport board.
Perhaps I should put the actual details of the increase on record. The higher fares agreed to by the companies last fall, called the Chandler fares, become effective on June 1 and remain effective until July 15, 1963. From July 16, 1963, the one way economy class fares will be reduced by $7, and the entire agreement expires on March 31, 1964. The net effect could perhaps be best illustrated by giving a few figures. The Chandler fare increase on a north Atlantic round trip would amount to about $27. The new fares that were agreed to, and which have now been approved, involve an increase of about $13.

subtopic: CANADIAN AGREEMENT TO FARE INCREASES ON ATLANTIC ROUTE
speechtext:
May I ask a supplementary question. In view of the fact that several members as well as myself were led to believe the Canadian authorities were going to stick to their position, I wonder if the

minister could tell us the factors that led them to negotiate a compromise instead of holding to their position which, as the minister said, was quite legal and would have resulted in our air carriers having the low fares on the Atlantic route.

subtopic: CANADIAN AGREEMENT TO FARE INCREASES ON ATLANTIC ROUTE
speechtext: Perhaps it would not be satisfactory to give a full answer on orders of the day; perhaps the answer should be more carefully worked out. However, I should indicate very clearly that for Canada to maintain its position on the old rates when all the air line companies and all the other countries had agreed to the compromise would have presented great difficulty and created chaotic conditions in the operation of international air lines. In addition, apparently the hon. member missed the significance of the fact that this new agreement expires on March 31, 1964, and this will afford an opportunity of perfecting the machinery for fixing these international air rates before the expiry of the agreement. I believe the hon. member will agree that is a most fortunate thing.

subtopic: CANADIAN AGREEMENT TO FARE INCREASES ON ATLANTIC ROUTE
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Will it be possible for Canada to revert to its original position at the end of the time mentioned by the minister?

subtopic: CANADIAN AGREEMENT TO FARE INCREASES ON ATLANTIC ROUTE
speechtext: We hope to get lower fares.

As hon. members will recall, Weldon Chan, a Chinese gentleman, came to Canada in 1958 as a visitor with his wife and their three year old daughter. They were to stay with Mrs. Chan's father in Vancouver for a few months. Chan subsequently applied to be admitted as a landed immigrant. His application was denied by an immigration board of inquiry, and on May 8, 1959, he and his family were ordered deported. An application to the immigration appeal board was dismissed, and the matter was subsequently reviewed by the the then minister of immigration who declined to quash the deportation order.
In order to avoid deportation, Chan went into hiding. His wife and daughter remained with Mrs. Chan's father in Vancouver, and
Inquiries of the Ministry no attempt appears to have been made since that time to deport the wife and daughter.
I have now had the chance to review the matter fully and to reach a decision in the light of all present factors and circumstances. Since this was a purely ministerial decision, I sincerely hope that my decision will not be interpreted as an implied criticism of the decisions made in this matter by my two predecessors at the times at which they were respectively made.
I have now decided, should Weldon Chan choose to surrender himself, to issue a permit under section 8 of the Immigration Act authorizing him and his family to stay in Canada for a period of 12 months, which is the maximum period allowed under the act for any such single permit. This would render possible the immediate reunion of the family, and allow the Chan family to take the necessary steps during this period to finally adjust their status as immigrants.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister) moved:
speechtext:
That a special committee be appointed to consider matters relating to defence and to report from time to time its observations and opinions thereon that the committee have power to send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses; that it be empowered to adjourn from place to place; that standing order 67 be suspended in relation to the committee; and that the committee consist of 18 members to be designated by the house at a later date.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution which has just been read to the house implements a pledge that we on this side have made. If accepted by the house it would carry out a proposal that was put by us to the house over the years when we were in opposition.
The resolution refers to a committee to consider matters relating to defence. There is no limitation in the resolution with regard to any such matters though, of course, there is always the limitation imposed by security considerations when this house or a committee of this house discusses defence. The resolution provides that the committee shall report to the house from time to time on matters relating to defence; that it shall have power to send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses; that it be empowered to adjourn from place to place. That means the committee can travel to defence installations and other places which it might be important to visit in connection with the business the committee is doing.
According to the terms of the resolution the committee should consist of 18 members to be designated by the house at a later date. I understand there have been discussions-and this was referred to last night 28902-5-301
Appointment of Defence Committee by my colleague, the leader of the house- among the representatives of the various parties, and the suggestion has been made that it would lead to an improvement in the basis of the representation of all parties on this committee of the number could be increased from 18 to 24. I am informed that this suggestion received unanimous approval on the part of those who were considering it. Therefore, though this would require the unanimous consent of the house, I make the suggestion that when this resolution is being considered the figure "18" be amended to read "24". If that is agreed to by the house, the committee will be considered as having 24 rather than 18 members.
I do not propose to detain hon. members very long in speaking to this resolution. I shall have an opportunity at the end of the debate to deal with any points which may arise during the discussion on the nature of the committee and its work. But I wish to make it clear at the beginning that a committee of this kind to deal with defence matters, if it is accepted, does not mean that it will be substituting in any way for the responsibility of the house itself in considering these matters. It would certainly be no substitute for the responsibility which the government must have in the making of decisions in regard to defence, the same responsibility which it has in making decisions on other aspects of policy.
Therefore I should like to make it clear at the outset that in recommending this committee it is not the intention of the government in any way, shape or form that, in the words of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) on May 21, as reported at page 114 of Hansard, it should be used "to give the government a chance to evade its responsibilities". No government can evade its responsibilities in the matter of defence or in any other field by the establishment of a committee. It is the purpose in setting up committees of this house to assist the government of the day in discharging its responsibilities; to convey information to the government and to give the government advice; to make recommendations to the government, if thought fit. But in the last analysis, under our parliamentary system of responsible government the government must remain responsible for any decisions taken.

Would the Prime Minister allow a question? The constitutional statement he has just made is one with which there can be no disagreement. But is it intended, and is it in contemplation by the government, that this committee shall have the right to make recommendations regarding policy?

Appointment of Defence Committee

I was coming to that. But I think there should be no limitation on the right of this committee to make recommendations on any matter within its terms of reference, and by "any matter" I do not exclude policy.
Does the Prime Minister include policy?

I will come to that if the right hon. gentleman will be patient. In the past the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the members of his party when they were in office opposed the establishment of a committee of the house to discuss defence policy. The ground for that opposition was that in their view a committee of this kind, considering defence policy, would interfere with and perhaps cut across the responsibility of the government in these matters to which I have just referred. The Leader of the Opposition took the position while in office and, indeed, when he was in opposition earlier, that no committee could even discuss defence policy because defence policy was the responsibility of government and government should not delegate this responsibility to a committee.
I have before me statements made by the right hon. gentleman and, as he has mentioned the subject, I might say that statements along similar lines, though with some qualifications, were made previously by Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent when he was prime minister, in 1951. However, in 1958 when there was a discussion in this chamber about the setting up of a defence committee, the right hon. gentleman now the Leader of the Opposition had this to say on May 30, as reported on page 681 of Hansard of that date. He was discussing a defence committee:
The only forbidden field, and it must remain so, will be that of government policy.
That was to be a forbidden field as far as the work of the defence committee was concerned. They could talk about expenditures, expenditures which had been made, but they could not discuss defence policy. More recently the right hon. gentleman reiterated his opposition to defence policy being discussed in a defence committee when he said, as reported on page 1889 of Hansard for November 22, 1962:
In so far as defence policy is concerned, as in the past when the hon. gentleman was a member of the former government, so today, and so, generally, throughout the free world, questions of policy are not submitted to committees.
I must note that the statement that throughout the free world questions of defence policy are not submitted to committees is an all embracing statement and one which is not accurate, because the United States is

still in the free world and there defence policies are not only submitted to congressional committees but they are very often decided in congressional committee.
I was referring to the parliamentary free world.

The right hon. gentleman says he was referring to the free world in which the parliamentary system of government is in effect. So far as we are concerned on this side of the house, we did not accept that position when we were in opposition. We did not accept the position that a defence committee should be limited in this way. Now that we are in office we do not accept this today. We are putting this committee forward in exactly the same terms and with the same intentions that we had three, four or five years back when we advocated a defence policy committee.
May I ask the Prime Minister whether such a committee has been set up before in Canada, particularly in the regime of Mr. St. Laurent?

No, Mr. Speaker, I do not think a committee of the kind envisaged in this resolution has been set up, although I speak subject to correction. Certainly it has not been set up while I have been a member of the House of Commons. But I am proposing that a committee of this kind be set up now with the approval of the House of Commons. In making that proposal I am being consistent in what I said in this house when I was in opposition. In the course of the throne speech as far back as January, 1960 I was asked by the then prime minister the following question, as recorded on page 48 of Hansard:
Does the hon. gentleman suggest that any committee under our system should discuss policy?
My reply was:
It certainly could, Mr. Speaker, if it were set up for this purpose. It could bring in recommendations, get advice on policy and ask the minister about policy questions. It certainly could discuss policy.
And I take that position today, Mr. Speaker. Then last October 1, 1962 I said in this house, as reported on page 73 of Hansard:
What we should have had years ago, and what we fought for in this house, is a defence committee on policy where we could try to find out the principles upon which the government is acting in defence matters. We have never been able to do that, but when a Liberal government takes over that will be done.
I might say parenthetically, Mr. Speaker, that we are now proposing that this should be done by this committee. I went on to say:
The defence policy will be examined by a committee in the House of Commons in the way it should be examined-

-that is if we had the responsibility of setting up such a committee-
-in a way it has not been examined since this government-
-that is the Conservative government-
-took office.
That is what we are proposing in the terms of this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, might I interrupt the Prime Minister at this stage? He has now described the ambit of this committee. Would he object to an amendment so it may be made perfectly clear that the special committee to be appointed is to consider matters relating to defence, and to report from time to time its observations and opinions thereon, including recommendations as to policy? In view of the fact that he stated that those words are inherent and that that idea is inherent in the definition, which I submit they are not, would he, in order to make the matter perfectly clear, be prepared to accept an amendment in those terms?

I have already said that in the terms of this resolution there is no limitation on the work of this committee in respect to all matters relating to defence. I have always indicated to the right hon. gentleman that in matters relating to defence we include in this resolution defence policy. I have indicated that that will presumably make the resolution unacceptable to my hon. friend if he follows the course he has followed in the past, when he has taken the position on behalf of his party and on behalf of the former government that it is inappropriate for a defence committee even to discuss policy, let alone to make recommendations on policy. We would assume that there would be no limitation this time on the committee which we are proposing to set up; but if in the course of this discussion an amendment is moved on this or on any other subject, that amendment will naturally be considered by the government when it sees the terms of such amendment.
Mr. Speaker, what I want to emphasize again is something which I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, that in setting up a committee of this kind to discuss, if it sees fit, defence policy matters and, if it sees fit, to make recommendations to the government of the day on defence policy questions, it does not interfere with the responsibility upon the government of making decisions in regard to those recommendations or any other matters of defence policy. Also, it does not interfere with the right of parliament itself, in committee of the whole and in discussion of the defence estimates, to reject decisions or to reject any matter of defence policy which may be put before it.
30,	1963
Appointment of Defence Committee
The previous government, in the defence committees which it set up, permitted examination only of expenditures. In the main committee, the most important committee, which was set up in 1960, the committee of that day was authorized to look into the expenditures which had already been made, and it was only later that the terms of reference of that committee were changed to enable it to look into expenditures which were proposed. If hon. members read, as I am sure many who took part in the discussions have read, the minutes of the committee on defence expenditures of 1960, they will realize how difficult indeed it was for a minister of defence, a minister of the crown, in the examination to which he was subjected in the committee on expenditures, to refrain from discussing policy. Indeed, he did not attempt to refrain, because it was quite impossible, in answering questions on defence expenditures, not to give the government's view on policy matters. So perhaps by making it clear that policy matters can be discussed in this committee we are not departing, in effect, very far from the position taken by the former minister of defence himself in 1960 when he appeared before the committee.
It has been said by my right hon. friend- and I have repeated some of his statements today-that it is not proper for a committee on defence to discuss defence policy, and that this cuts across our system of parliamentary, constitutional, responsible government. I would point out, as I have indeed pointed out in the past in this house, that there is a good analogy to the proposed defence committee in the committee on external affairs. The committee on external affairs has been in existence now for a good many years. There has never been any limitation on the right of that committee to discuss questions of foreign policy. There has never been any limitation on the right of members of that committee to examine the secretary of state for external affairs on foreign policy questions. And I do not think that committee has been considered as an agency which has prejudiced in any way our system of parliamentary government, where the government must take the responsibility of making decisions and then announce them in the House of Commons.
When I talk about a defence committee of this kind I do not mean, and the terms of the resolution should not be interpreted to mean, that the right of the members of that committee to summon witnesses extends to serving officers. I think it would be improper for serving officers to appear; but

Appointment of Defence Committee if they were summoned before the committee, the right of the committee to summon anyone does not extend to the obligation of a serving officer to give any information on policy matters. Policy matters in a committee of this kind, as was the case in the committee on external affairs, can be discussed. The government can be questioned on policy, but the spokesman of the government on policy matters should be a political spokesman of the government. In the case of the external affairs committee that spokesman has been the secretary of state for external affairs.
If I may be pardoned a personal reference, Mr. Speaker, I recall that when I was deputy minister of external affairs I appeared before the committee, but I was not asked questions about policy. At least occasionally I may have been asked a question on policy by inadvertence, but if I was I always replied that it was a policy matter which naturally the minister would deal with when he appeared before the committee, and then I took note of the question and submitted it to the minister. Then later when I appeared before the committee on external affairs as secretary of state for external affairs, my right hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition, who was a member of the committee, will remember how the committee itself roamed far and wide over the whole field of foreign policy, and that the minister, I think it is right to say, did not show any reluctance to discuss with the committee any aspects of foreign policy on behalf of the government.
Subject always, of course, to military security considerations, I suggest that is the way that a committee on defence should and could operate; that the ministers of defence would appear before the committee and if there were questions on government policy that members wished to ask, if there were exchanges of views on government policy that members wished to bring about with the spokesman of the government, it would be the obligation of the minister to give the committee all the information he possibly could and take notice of the views of the members of the committee, and in due course the government will take notice of any recommendations which it cares to make.
There is no reason, as I see it, why a committee of this kind should not exchange views on the principles of defence policy; on the reasons for the expenditures made consequent upon defence policy; on the contributions that Canada has made to the NATO alliance, for instance; on changes in defence policy that the Canadian government in due course might be wise to make; on our continental defence policy; on our relations with the United States on continental and joint defence. It seems to me it would not only

be possible but also helpful to have matters of that kind discussed in a committee of this kind, and in such a discussion the only spokesman for the government would be, of course, a minister of the crown.
This does not mean that in such a defence committee the deputy minister and perhaps even the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee should not be able to appear if they were required to answer questions of fact and to answer questions on which information was required that did not entrench on policy considerations. I would, however, believe that it would be wrong if, apart from the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee, serving officers were asked to appear before the committee and were questioned in a way which would embarrass them as officers of the services. I think the committee could be very useful indeed in the field of policy without that kind of investigation which is so common to congressional committees in Washington, where I know the system is very different indeed but where I believe-perhaps I should not say this-harm can be done by asking for the views of serving officers which run counter to the views of their civilian chiefs, who are responsible and should be responsible for decisions on policy.
It is also provided in the resolution that the committee, if it so desires, can send for outside witnesses. By that I mean witnesses who would not be serving officers of the armed forces or civil servants of the government of Canada, who would naturally appear before the committee only to give information in regard to matters of fact. But outside witnesses whom the committee felt by their knowledge and experience could contribute to the work of the committee would, it seems to me, be very appropriate witnesses for the committee to summon if it so desired.
That is what we in the government have in mind in putting this resolution before the house. If the house sees fit to accept the resolution and the committee of 24 members is set up representing all parties in the house, I think it can serve a very useful purpose in clarifying the ideas of members of the committee and, through members of the committee, clarifying the ideas of the country on the difficult, complicated and at times dangerous questions of defence. It can also be useful in the recommendations it may see fit to make in the same way that committees make recommendations on other subjects to the government of the day.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am very happy indeed to put this resolution to the house for its consideration.

Am I to understand that by unanimous consent and without any special

motion the resolution is to be amended to the effect that the committee shall consist of 24 members instead of 18?
Agreed.

May I ask the Prime Minister a question which I intended to put before he took his seat? To what extent would the recommendations of this committee be binding on the government, if at all? Maybe I missed that point in his address, and if I did I apologize.

Legally and constitutionally they would not be binding in any way, because that would indeed contravene our system of parliamentary responsible government where the government must be responsible for decisions. But I should think they would be of great interest to and have an influence on the government in making the decisions that it would have to make on matters of policy.
Did the Prime Minister say that Senate committees in the United States make policy recommendations which are binding on the government there? I should like clarification of that point.

The congressional system is entirely different, and the powers of congressional committees are much greater in respect of the binding nature of their recommendations than the powers of any parliamentary committee. I am not suggesting nor is the government suggesting, in recommending this resolution, that we adopt the United States practice in this regard.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to ask a question first. Is the Minister of National Defence not going to give us an outline of government policy at the present time so the debate may develop in an orderly fashion?

I will not be giving a statement of government policy on defence at the present time. I would, I presume, if the committee so desired, make an opening statement at the committee's deliberations which would more or less start the proceedings.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has approached this problem in the most halfhearted manner I have ever seen. During the course of the election campaign and in the last session of parliament we heard endless talk about the necessity of a committee to discuss and determine-that was the inference-defence policy, and various statements have already been made in the house before
Appointment of Defence Committee we reached this particular point in our proceedings about what was going to be done.
We have now reached the item on the order paper; a very lukewarm, halfhearted presentation is made by the Prime Minister, with regard to his much vaunted committee on defence, and neither the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) nor the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin) is prepared to give us a statement with regard to the government's policy at the present time.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, would it be in order for a spokesman of the government to make a statement on defence policy in connection with this resolution?

The whole purpose of this debate is to set up a committee, and the discussion should be relevant to setting up the committee. Members may indicate from time to time, of course, subjects that might be considered by the committee, but I do not think a general debate is called for at the present time. I will not go any further at the moment, but I have considerable authority for what I have just said.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I know you have not made a ruling yet and I should like to say something. Under all the circumstances, and particularly in view of the far ranging discussion on the part of the Prime Minister, I feel that in the consideration of a matter as important as defence, discussion should not be limited in the course of this debate which has as its purpose as you have said, and properly so, the setting up of a committee.
But I do feel that unless there is going to be reasonable freedom in consideration of this whole problem, then this debate will simply be a means whereby the important matter of defence will be given to a committee and, inferentially, the House of Commons will be denied the opportunity of discussing this matter. I hope that there will be give and take on both sides in this connection, and that Your Honour will not be required to make a ruling that would deny to members of this house the right to discuss a subject that has received widespread attention and deserves to be dealt with by members of this house in some detail.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I speak to the point of order that has been raised? I agree with the right hon. gentleman that if any attempt were made to restrict this debate merely to the narrow question, should a committee be set up or should it not, it would be unduly restrictive. The government has no such thought. At the same time, sir, Your Honour's

Appointment of Defence Committee predecessor, Mr. Speaker Michener, gave rulings on several occasions-on one occasion the ruling was made against me, so I remember it quite well-that the whole policy with respect to the subject matter being referred to a committee should not be discussed in the house because that was the purpose of the committee, to have the matter discussed there. I am speaking from recollection, but my recollection is rather vivid in this particular case since the ruling was made against me.
That was not unusual in your case.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No; I think, as a matter of fact, that my score was almost as bad as the right hon. gentleman's.
As I was saying before the amiable interruption by the right hon. gentleman, it has always been the practice to permit hon. members to suggest subjects and to give reasons why there should be certain priority relating to subjects to be discussed by a committee. However, since committees are set up for the purpose of considering a matter, and 1 think Your Honour's predecessors have so ruled, it has always been clearly understood that it would be quite wrong to have a debate in the house on the subject itself that the committee is being asked to consider, and before the committee has considered it. When the committee has considered it and made its report, the report is then before hon. gentlemen and at that stage there is an opportunity for debating the report of the committee and to deal with everything that the committee itself decided.

May I add one further word? I think what the hon. gentleman has said pretty well represents the situation. It is a distinction without a difference so far as I am concerned, and I think as we proceed on the basis of what he has indicated is the desire of the government, not to prevent the opposition placing before the house its views, I am sure that there will be that degree of give and take which will permit a wide discussion.

I should like to speak to the point of order, Mr. Speaker. I think it would be a mistake if too narrow an interpretation were placed on the terms of this resolution. I believe the house has to keep in mind that, prior to parliament meeting, the government made it clear that there would be an early opportunity for discussing general defence questions. Once the committee is set up, in view of the fact that these questions are being discussed in the committee, we may be debarred from discussing general defence matters in the house.
It seems to me that this is almost the only opportunity that will be presented for some

time for a general discussion of defence policy, as was promised by the government prior to parliament convening. While no one, I am sure, wants to wander far afield, I feel it would be a mistake to narrowly limit the debate on this motion to the question merely of whether a committee should be set up or should not be set up.

Speaking to the point of order, may I say that the right hon. gentleman used as an argument for a wide discussion, the fact that I had ranged, as he said, over the entire field of defence policy. I did not talk about defence policy at all in my short remarks. I confined my remarks to the resolution question, the nature of the committee and the terms of reference to the committee, what I thought it might do and might not do. While I am not, of course, objecting in any way, Mr. Speaker, to the remarks that have been made about some latitude being given in a debate of this kind on a proposal to set up a committee, I would say in answer to the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that far from restricting debate on this matter there has already been a wide discussion on a point decided earlier. There will be a supply motion shortly when the whole question of defence can be raised, and there will be the defence estimates before long. Therefore, there is no disposition on the part of the government to limit the widest possible discussion of defence policy at every appropriate opportunity.

I agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in general. However, I would not want to be taken as accepting the view that the fact general defence problems had been submitted to a committee would debar this house from discussing the question of defence at any time.
However, I feel we are pretty well in agreement now, and I would not want to press the matter any further.

Perhaps I can conclude the matter by quoting some excellent remarks by a previous Speaker made on March 23, 1960, as found on page 2371 of Hansard for that date:
To conclude the matter I would ask the co-operation of the house in keeping these debates on motions to appoint committees within the appropriate limited bounds. I do not propose to be unduly restrictive but I suggest we follow the rules unless the house determines otherwise. If the house decides it wants a general debate, that is done by unanimous consent, and that is a different case. Otherwise, however, we will attempt to keep within the rules.
It seems to me we have a general understanding of the problem.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is rather fortunate that the Secretary of State was present this afternoon to save the Prime Minister from error when he was almost on the point of preventing us discussing the very subject he says we should be discussing.
I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. gentleman is once again falling into his customary practice of misinterpreting and distorting remarks made from this side of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
I suggest he is completely wrong in what he has said, once again, even though he has no documents to support him this time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Now you are in trouble.
I think the word "distort" is parliamentary, and if it is I apply it to the right hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The words which the Prime Minister has used are a reflection and will have to be withdrawn.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He said, referring to me, "-my customary practice of distorting-" what other word did he use?
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: -distorting and giving misinformation to the house.

I think I can resolve the difficulty. If there is any hint of restriction at all, it is due to myself. In my capacity as Speaker, it is my duty to point out what the rules of the house are. If the members of the house generally feel that there should be a slightly wider discussion, I do not see any particular objection to that, provided it is kept within the bounds of reason.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Before we get to that wider discussion, I may say that I am discussing a point of privilege concerning accusations made by the Prime Minister that I have distorted or, in other words, misled the house. This is not an accusation that can be made and substantiated by the Prime Minister, and those words are unparliamentary and will have to be withdrawn.

On the question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I said that the hon. gentleman had distorted and misrepresented what I have said. If I had said the hon. gentleman had deliberately distorted and misrepresented, it would be a different matter, but of course he did not do it deliberately. He did not even know what he was doing.
Appointment of Defence Committee

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Grit party is continuing to show it will destroy itself by its arrogance.
I had hoped that the Minister of National Defence would have accepted my invitation to give us a statement for the direction of the committee. They are intent now on setting up a committee, but let us have some direction as to the subject matters that committee would undertake to look at. Let us have something from the Minister of National Defence. He has now been in office for some considerable time. The Prime Minister speaks for him, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but we hear nothing from the minister in charge. The Associate Minister of National Defence has virtually disappeared from sight.
He is dealing with government business.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
This is a most unfortunate thing in dealing with a department of such great importance as the Department of National Defence.
I started off some time ago to draw attention to the fact that the Prime Minister has very halfheartedly introduced this resolution to set up a committee, and I suggest to you, sir, that in the minds of hon. members of the house, and in the minds of the public, there has been a different concept of what was to be attempted with the committee, than that given to us this afternoon.
Away back in January the Prime Minister, then the leader of the opposition, in the celebrated speech when he changed his position used these words:
We should set up a small select committee on defence policy. Through that committee we should try to work out a defence policy on the broadest possible national basis.
There is no word of defence policy in the resolution to set up this committee. It is one of those resolutions that evades the matter. Instead of using the words "defence policy," those words used in the last session, during the election campaign and in the turnabout speech at Scarborough, we get the words "matters relating to defence," which is subject to all sorts of interpretation. The committee could spend its whole time on defence expenditures, of course with some profit to public knowledge. It could spend its whole time on travelling around to various bases. This is the sop which is held out. There are going to be some trips. This special committee is to visit this base and that base, but there is nothing about defence policy in the resolution.
Let us be very clear as to the impression that was given to the public. As recorded in

Appointment of Defence Committee Hansard of May 21 at page 109, the Prime Minister used these words:
-we would be bringing forward very shortly a resolution to set up a defence committee to discuss defence policy.
This is the type of information that has gone out over the radio and television, and through the newspapers-a committee to discuss defence policy, but we get the statement today that it is "to consider matters relating to defence."
On May 17, as recorded at page 13 of Hansard for that date, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) asked the Minister of National Defence this question:
For the benefit of the house I would like him to define what is meant by the "modern arms weapons" that are to be made available for the Canadian armed forces.
In his reply the minister said:
-in view of the fact that a resolution will be introduced shortly to set up a special select committee on defence problems I think that would be the best time to discuss these matters in detail.
Mr. Speaker, we are at that very stage now. In effect the minister said, "Save your questions until we are setting up the committee on defence problems, and when we are setting up that committee, that will be the best time to discuss these matters in detail." That is why I asked the Minister of National Defence to let us have his opinions with regard to these matters.
I suggest to the house that the impression created over the last several months was that we were to have a committee on defence policy, and as reported at page 308 of Hansard for May 27 the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) said:
As members of the house know, the Prime Minister has announced in the house ... the government's intention to conduct a national review of defence policy and to set up without delay a parliamentary committee as part of that process-
A national review of defence policy was to be the work of the committee, and that is the impression that has been created. There are some people in the country who will consider that they have been misled by this great blowup, and when hon. members of the other parties speak I am sure they will say they were expecting a committee to consider defence policy.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? May I ask him if he is prepared to move an amendment to include after the words "matters relating to defence" the words "including defence policy."

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: These matters will be considered.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would think that the Prime Minister, who has already moved a resolution that was badly prepared, should now correct it and he should have in it his words with regard to defence policy. When the Prime Minister was asked the question during the course of his remarks, he hedged. He read out this phrase "matters relating to defence" and he said this would be as wide as you like, but of course with certain reservations, you know, with regard to security matters. Then he said, "You understand it is the responsibility of the government to make decisions."
The Leader of the Opposition asked him if it included policy, and we did not get an answer to that.
The answer was yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
He was asked if it was included in this way, and he replied that the committee may discuss anything it likes. Then, Mr. Speaker, he casts scorn on committees that have been set up in the past, committees set up for specific purposes. For example there was the committee on defence expenditures, and once you get into defence expenditures you do not have much time for questions of policy. That committee met in 1951 and 1952, and in 1960, when we were on defence expenditures, and there was a restriction on the work of the committee so that it would not spend its whole time on other related matters. But now the Prime Minister says, "Oh, yes, you may discuss anything with regard to defence."
I think we will have to be very sure we are not prevented in this house from discussing these matters pertaining to defence, after the committee has been set up. This is the danger I see in some of this, in the wording of this resolution. Well, where do we stand on the question of defence policy? What is the policy of the present government? What happens when the committee is discussing some matter dealing with defence policy and discovers that the decision has already been made by the government? Then it goes on just discussing it and says whether it was a good decision or a bad one. What will happen if during the course of this committee the government is faced with some problem relating to defence on which a decision is required? Will that be referred to the committee for consideration before the government makes its decision, or will the committee be kept in the dark with regard to that on the grounds of security? I very much fear that this is exactly what will happen. The committee will not be given the information with regard to decisions which the government-as any government has to do-will have to make concerning defence matters. But then it will be able to discuss these matters later, according to the Prime

Minister. He rather suggested that without a committee to discuss matters such as this we would not have the same opportunity here; and finally, when pressed, he had to admit that there would be opportunities to discuss this matter in the house on the consideration of estimates, supply motions and things of that nature. We will insist on our rights here in the House of Commons to discuss defence at every opportune moment. We will continue to press the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) with questions, and I hope he will not attempt to defer these questions to the special committee on defence. I warn him in advance that this will not be acceptable to the House of Commons. I have been suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that this House of Commons and the people generally will not be satisfied with the committee as proposed by the Prime Minister, a committee which is not even given a good send-off by the Minister of National Defence.
I am quite prepared to admit that no greater problem faces any country at the present time than this question of defence, of war or peace. I am quite prepared to admit that Canada has a very serious problem to consider with regard to defence. These things should be looked at. They can be looked at by the House of Commons. They can be examined by a committee; we can have two or three committees. But nevertheless the government itself has to approach these problems. The government has to make decisions and they have to announce those decisions. Let us deal with them and let the public generally know what is going on. The problem of defence has been a major problem, and apparently will continue to be a major problem, for our country and other countries for a very long time. It is a very expensive burden resting on our country. A very large part of our budget each year has to be devoted to defence expenditure. Naturally we are interested in seeing whether that money is spent wisely. We are interested in seeing what changes are desired as time goes on. If the committee had been set up for policy matters, it might have suggested to the government before a decision was made what changes should be incorporated in our defence set-up. But I doubt very much if it will have that opportunity.
Despite the heavy expenditure over the years on defence, peace has been maintained in the world since the second world war, in so far as a world conflagration is concerned. Although everyone as a taxpayer has some misgivings with regard to the heavy expenditures on defence, nevertheless I think we must really consider that it is and has been a form of insurance. We have not had
Appointment of Defence Committee an outbreak of world war since the conclusion of the second world war, and we hope that with the work of the alliances with which we are associated, the work of the United Nations, and so on, peace will continue to prevail. This is our hope, because a world conflict would be much more destructive than anything we have seen in the past. Therefore, although defence expenditures have placed a very heavy burden on the Canadian taxpayer, we have received the value of insurance against world conflict from those expenditures.
When it comes to the application of that money and how it should best be expended we enter into a realm of controversy. The committee on defence will not be able to deal adequately with the problems that will confront us unless we have in advance here an outline of some of those problems. That is why I hope we will have such an outline from the government side of the house before the conclusion of this debate. Let us outline in general terms the problems which face us, and then the committee, when it gets down to work, can examine those problems and come up with its findings.
One of the things that strikes me as I read about defence matters and examine the record is the tremendous change that takes place almost every year in defence affairs. The rapidity of technological change in defence matters is almost too great for the lay mind to grasp. We find that the situation as it applied 15, 10, or 5 years ago is rapidly out of date. We seem to be moving into a new age, and some of the weapons which are being devised at the present time are a bit beyond the comprehension of most of us. I am particularly struck with the changes which have occurred over the years.
The U.S. News and World Report has given very valuable service to the public from time to time in indicating the burden which is being carried by the members of the NATO alliance, the manpower requirements and things of that nature. I note in the magazine of January 21, 1963, where the article is discussing and comparing the burden borne by the United States and that borne by its allies, that most unfortunately Canada has been omitted from the list of NATO allies. Had Canada's contribution in money been entered in the column devoted to that subject, we would have been shown as fifth among the NATO allies in the amount of money we are spending on national defence. This amount, as appears in the estimates recently tabled, is in the order of $1,600,000,000. If in the list showing manpower provided by the various countries Canada had been listed, as she should have been listed, we would have been shown as seventh in the group of

Appointment of Defence Committee the 14 countries which do make a substantial contribution to the NATO alliance. Canada has been playing her part with men and with money and has no need to take second place to anyone in this alliance with regard to the effort she is putting forward.
I think at this time a review of our requirements in this atomic age is essential. Once again, in this magazine, U.S. News and World Report we get a picture of the changing concept of defence as far as the United States and NATO are concerned. These changes are really very rapid. In the issue of March 25, 1963, there is an article-it appears to be semi-official-which shows the four stages which are now in progress with respect to United States defence arrangements. Step one is the dismantling of the bases which were built all around Russia after the second world war. Nuclear bombers and intermediate missiles are being withdrawn from England, Italy, Turkey, Morocco and elsewhere. Step two provides for smaller nuclear weapons to be withdrawn from Europe and an effort is being made to dissuade NATO allies from building their own atomic forces. As part of step three, around the world United States ground forces and tactical air units are to be gradually withdrawn to United States soil. United States treaty commitments will preferably be met in future by "fire brigade" forces based in that country.
These are some of the developments which have taken place already or which are being considered. Step number four comes down to this-that the mainstay of future United States defence becomes nuclear missiles, mainly Minuteman and Polaris, based on United States soil or in United States submarines where the president can maintain absolute control free from political or other interference from any foreign country.
These are illustrations of one aspect of the changes that are taking place. The other significant change within the last few years has been the piling up of nuclear missiles at a rate which is simply staggering. Again, I am dependant on the U.S. News and World Report, and this time I should like to read a few sentences from the issue of March 18, 1963:
Missiles approaching 60,000 in number will be added to the U.S. arsenal of weapons this year. Missiles are being turned out in the U.S. at a rate of 3.9 billion dollars worth a year.
The article continues under a heading "A Missile for Every Job", and charts are given of the missiles which are listed. There is apparently no security attached to this matter. The big missiles are the intercontinental ballistic missiles which have a range of up to 9,000 miles. The United States also has ready for use an Atlas missile, 129 of which


are in place now at 11 bases all within the United States. There is also a type called Titan I and II with a range of 9,000 miles. All 54 of the planned Titan I missiles are now completed and in place at five bases. Fifty four Titan II's are now coming. They also have the Minuteman, 60 of which are now in place on bases in Montana. Five more bases are under way and it is planned to produce 950 of these missiles in the next four years. Then there is the Polaris which has a range of between 1,200 and 2,500 miles. One hundred and forty four missiles of this type are now aboard nine submarines. They intend to have 656 of these missiles aboard 41 submarines. These, Mr. Speaker, are all large missiles.
Looking further down the list I note there is the Thor, with a range of 1,500 miles. Sixty of these based in Britain are being withdrawn. Another intermediate range missile, the Jupiter, was, or is, in Italy and Turkey. It is now being withdrawn and replaced by Polaris missiles. The next missile listed is the Mace which was in place in West Germany. I presume that this, too, is being withdrawn. Those are the big missiles. Then we come to the missiles intended for defence against enemy aircraft, and there are nine of them listed in this magazine together with their ranges and so on. All of them, apparently, are operating. In addition to these are nuclear missiles for use by battlefield troops and eight of these are listed-the Pershing, the Redstone, the Honest John, the Little John, the Sergeant, the Lacrosse, the Shillelagh and the Davy Crockett. Then, as a further indication that we are well into the missile age, we find missiles which can be fired from airplanes against enemy planes. These include the Sidewinder, the Genie, the Falcon and the Sparrow III.
In addition, they are trying to develop a missile to strike down other missiles, the Nike-Zeus. The list is not yet complete. There are anti-submarine missiles-the Subroc, the Asroc and the Alpha. The magazine contains a short description of the Skybolt missile designed to be discharged at some considerable distance from its target. Production of the Skybolt has recently been discontinued. In the same class, though, is the Hound Dog which can be launched 600 miles from its target by the airplane which carries it. Then, having a shorter range, is the Bullpup which can be launched against surface targets.
That is just a quick rundown of the missiles now available in this missile age, and the number of these missiles is multiplying at a rapid rate. Their destructive capacity staggers the imagination. These are matters which will have to be considered by the

special committee before it can reach any conclusion pertaining to Canada's defence now or in the future, or before it can advise the government with regard to policy.
As I have said, the destructive power of these missiles is simply tremendous. One has to learn the nuclear jargon before he can begin to appreciate this fact. The Winnipeg Tribune published a series of articles to inform the public, and a collection of these articles has appeared under the title "The Nuclear Primer". I believe there are 24 of these articles which, together, give a great deal of information in popular phraseology which the average individual can understand. The article talks about the sizes of the various bombs available for use at the present time and compares them with the one which destroyed Hiroshima. The Hiroshima bomb was the equivalent of 20,000 tons of t.n.t. When that bomb was exploded the world stood aghast and Hiroshima was wiped out. Well, the warhead of the Honest John rocket which is the missile available to the batteries now in place in Europe, one of the smaller missiles in this missile age, is equivalent in size to the Hiroshima bomb, in other words to 20,000 tons of t.n.t. The smallest United States strategic warhead, that is, among the big missiles I was talking about, has a destructive force equal to 500,000 tons of t.n.t., namely, 25 of the bombs which fell on Hiroshima.
Human imagination finds it very hard to grasp that. Then the writers go on to mention horrifying figures as to the number of people who might be killed and wounded if a holocaust were to occur. President Kennedy estimates 175 million people would be casualties in the first round if there were an exchange of nuclear attacks between east and west. Premier Khrushchev says the dead and injured would be 800 million in the first 18 hours.
In the use of these terms-and they may come up-the kiloton has the explosive force of 1,000 tons of t.n.t. The Hiroshima bomb was 20 kilotons. The megaton bomb has the explosive force of 1 million tons of t.n.t. SAC bombers carry two 24-megaton bombs. The other day in this house reference was made to the bomb which might be carried by the Starfighters in the Canadian air division in Europe. This bomb was spoken of as being a megaton bomb.

My understanding is that there are several sizes of bombs which might be used by the Starfighters, and perhaps the minister might enlighten us in the future unless it is a security matter. The destructive capabilities of these bombs are simply tremendous.
The reason I draw these matters to the attention of the house is this. I think it is right to ask ourselves if we have not reached the limit of production of weapons of such destruction. Should we be spending more money to produce hundreds of thousands more weapons of this size? How great should be the deterrent? The deterrent has, in my opinion, prevented the outbreak of a world war. I do not stand here as a pacifist at all, but I would ask how great that deterrent should be. Somewhere there should be a ceiling, because you get this kill and overkill. How many times are you going to destroy a country? If it can be killed in the first thrust or attack you do not require the overkill. I am not opposed to a substantial deterrent, but I would ask the question-and this the committee may have to look at in the house- how great that deterrent should be, and then relate it to Canada's contribution to its armed forces in the NATO alliance.
These are questions which sensible people are asking. Is there any need for Canada to make any further contribution to the nuclear deterrent, or is that nuclear deterrent now great enough? If the United States continues to produce missiles by the thousands and continues to put them in these hardened bases underground where they cannot be destroyed on the surface, then one's conception of the use of the Canadian air force might be changed. Have we now reached the missile age where we do not need to use aeroplanes to carry bombs? On the other hand, people say it is a flexible method, because you can call back a man in an aeroplane which is carrying a bomb whereas, once you have let off a missile, it has gone for good and you cannot recall it. These are some of the problems which have to be considered.
The conclusion I have reached, although I, like others, require further information, is this, that in the last several years technological advance in the power of scientific destruction has grown so rapidly that a major overhaul and examination of defence requirements is necessary. Even if this results in changes and the scrapping of this or that weapon, it is no different from what has happened throughout this history of defence and warfare. Many an example could be given of a weapon which has been produced and then succeeded by something more efficient. As far back in Canadian history as the first world war you had the replacement of the

Appointment of Defence Committee Ross rifle by the Lee-Enfield, and there was a tremendous story about that. In the second world war you had the Grant tank of the United States replaced by the Sherman because it was a much more effective weapon. I can give you a dozen examples of a newer, more efficient weapon succeeding an older one where you simply had to write off the obsolete weapon. So I just make the point that we may seriously have to consider whether changes should be made, whether we should cut our losses. We might have to cut our losses and direct our defence effort along some other line.
I am not prepared to give my solution to that particular problem, but I think that, as sensible people, we have to look at it without getting emotionally disturbed. The danger which has happened over the last two or three years has been the stirring up of the emotions over some of these problems. I cannot subscribe to that at all, although I do not object to a little political warfare and never will. But in this sort of problem we must prepare our minds for certain changes.
This then will get us out of the field where we might have serious difficulties in the political warfare element, and we might be able to concentrate our minds on the exact problem. The committee would have to examine the present and future role of Canada's navy. There again, is it kill and overkill? Does the navy require nuclear weapons for the killing of enemy submarines? With regard to the army we have to consider whether the army requires nuclear weapons on the battlefield, and I do not think that we shall have to agree without careful consideration and examination to the request which may come from certain quarters. I think we can make this decision ourselves.
I think we have to consider whether it is not wiser for a country of our size to be in the so-called conventional arms field. I would seriously question whether, if there should be an attack by bombers on this north American continent-I very much doubt it because I think the bomber threat has just about gone; but assuming that there still is a bomber threat-the first intercept of the attacking bomber should be made by fighters armed with nuclear weapons. There might be a mistake, and I suggest that that mistake had better be made with the firing off of a conventional weapon so that you do not start a nuclear war. I think the greatest danger we face at the present time is mistake-[DOT] human error or failure. Someone might set off one of these nuclear bombs by error. I question whether with our army in Europe there should be any use of a nuclear weapon until the conventional side has reached the stage where it is no longer effective. But then,

once you get into the nuclear field, you cannot have a limited nuclear war: you have world destruction.
So I raise these questions about our army, navy and air force as to whether or not Canada's position and the assistance we offer in this peculiarly difficult field might not be better served by the use of conventional armed forces. We would be filling a role which is being asked for by various people who are saying that the NATO forces are unbalanced, too heavy on the nuclear deterrent side and not sufficient on the conventional arms side.
What is the role for a smaller country? I always become very annoyed when people suggest that Canada is not fulfilling her commitments or her role in this world because I have said often and I say again that Canada's record in world crises has been equalled by other nations, but not surpassed. We were a small nation of 8 million people in the first world war and had a casualty list of 60,000 killed. We were a nation of only 12 million people in the second world war with a casualty list of 40,000. One hundred thousand young Canadians have been killed in two world wars in my lifetime. What other country has made any greater sacrifice? The losses of life, so far as France and the United Kingdom are concerned, were perhaps greater in the first world war, but we have played our part as a nation.
Between wars we have played our part and we are playing our part now and living up to our commitments. My friends opposite have not found yet a commitment that we have not lived up to. We have suggested a re-examination of our commitments, expressed or implied, if you like to put it that way, and a re-examination of them may show that we should redirect our energies along some other line.

Without settling the question, I raise this point for the consideration of the committee. Our air division in Europe is being brought to completion. I do not need to reiterate that only one squadron has been reorganized at the present time, and a second squadron is in the process; but by the time it is finished 10 or 12 months from now there will be 144 Starfighter planes in the air division in Europe. I simply raise the question whether that is the best role for Canada. These planes will become part of the deterrent. They will be grounded except for practice flights, because you cannot and certainly should not attach a nuclear bomb to a plane and then start flying it around the country. The air division will be virtually grounded and will be out of action unless nuclear war breaks out. That is fine as a deterrent, and I have no objection to the use of a deterrent, but to my way of thinking this will incapacitate a great air force.
I would rather see our airmen more actively employed. I grant that they will have to make practice flights all the time, but they are being pinned down to a role where they are not in close support of an army and their task is simply as part of the deterrent. Their task becomes something like that of the SAC bombers of the United States bomber fleet.
Without answering or solving the question, I raise it for consideration. Is this the best use that can be made of Canadian airmen who are the best airmen in the world and have been ever since air forces were started in the first world war? As I say, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to provide that all workers coming under federal labour jurisdiction, and we all know that workers in this country come in some instances under federal and in some instances under provincial labour jurisdiction, shall get eight holidays a year with pay. I said I was going to deal very briefly with the terms of the bill itself, and I have kept that commitment. I should now like to say something about the significance of this bill being before us today, as it is the first piece of private members' legislation to be considered in this twenty sixth parliament. A great deal has been said in this house and in the press throughout the country about the desirability of making this parliament work. We have said from this comer of the house that we are prepared to give the government of the day a chance to bring forward its legislation, a chance to have that legislation considered, and when it is good we are prepared to support it. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is a two-way street. If the private members of all parties in this house are asked to co-operate with the government in seeing that its legislation might be considered and, where worthy, passed, then by the same token it is time that the government of the day co-operated with the private members in this house and made it possible for their proposals to receive consideration.
There are, on the order paper, 65 private members' bills at the present time. I suggest that these bills, covering a wide range of subjects as they do, represent a great deal of thought on the part of the people who have


been sent here by their constituents. In addition to private members' bills there are, of course, a great number of resolutions. Speaking of this bill of mine, which has been before the house on previous occasions, I would say it has met the same fate as many other private members' bills and resolutions: it has been talked out. I plead with this house, and in particular with the government not to do that today. I suggest that this bill coming first presents the government with a challenge to show that it means what it says about wanting this parliament to do a job of work; that it means what it says about wanting the procedures and practices of parliament to be updated so that this house will be more efficient. I suggest that if this bill is talked out, particularly if it is talked out by a member representing the government party, it means, in effect, that there is no change so far as the government's attitude towards parliament as a whole is concerned.
Most of the proposals that are on the order paper today have been put there by private members. They have done a lot of thinking; they have a lot of ideas, and I suggest that they should be considered. Both of them said they were speaking for their fellow members of the Liberal party. I remind them that there were some other related bills and other Liberals spoke to those bills. In fact, the present Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) spoke on one of them, and indicated that the Liberals were prepared to support this kind of progressive social legislation.
Well, Mr. Speaker, on both counts I make my appeal to the house, and I make it particularly to the government. There are at least two ways in which this could be done. One way, the way I would prefer, would bp for the house to let this motion for second reading come to a vote before six o'clock. of this bill. If it carried, the immediate result would be that the bill would be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations. I repeat that a government that has asked for co-operation to get its legislation through, and a government that has been assured by us and other groups that it is going to get that co-operation, has a responsibility in this five to six o'clock hour, on this 30th day of May, and on this 38th day of decision in the life of the present government.

I may say he neglected to say that although his proposals were not put into legislative form during the years when a Liberal government was in power, it remains a fact that Liberal governments both federal and provincial have, over the years, provided between 90 and 95 per cent of the good labour legislation which has been enacted. This, I feel sure, is beyond dispute.
We all congratulate the hon. member on having brought this subject again before us during the first session of the new parliament in which a Liberal government has taken over the administration. However, I think the hon. member who sponsors this bill should bear in mind the heavy program which lies ahead. We in the Liberal party do not expect to get through parliament all our proposed legislation within the next 60 days-the 60 days of decision as members opposite choose to call them. However, we envisage a large number of legislative proposals dealing with the welfare of all who labour in one field or another. The hon. member might recall that we have proposed to grant bargaining rights to all federal civil servants. It is true the Conservatives have intimated that they, too, are prepared to provide similar bargaining rights-but not when they were in a position to bring forward legislation to this end. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has said this is one of our proposals.
In addition, in answer to a question posed to him recently on the orders of the day, the Prime Minister said we are prepared to bring in a measure providing for a minimum wage
[Mr. Gray.l
in all federal undertakings. During the election campaign we said we were prepared to revise the entire labour code. This, of course, is bound to be an extensive undertaking. We have also said we intend to amend the act providing for vacations with pay. The terms of the present act provide for one week. This seems to be the very minimum of vacation which could be offered and, as I say, we have indicated we intend to move ahead in this field. In our revision of the labour code we propose also to provide for maximum hours of work in any working week.
I realize it would be gratifying to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre if we were to accept his bill holus-bolus at this time but I think that on reflection he will see the wisdom of providing for an over-all revision of labour questions as far as the federal jurisdiction is concerned.

The important thing in June of 1963 is to get people to work, to get legislation through which is going to provide jobs for people. That is the primary task which faces us, rather than providing ways of ensuring holidays and so on. There are still many hundreds of thousands who are looking for work.
I was interested in the short and concise speech made by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). It was interesting to note, and I noted it with pleasure because I am sure we will be calling upon his support when the government brings in an over-all revision of the labour acts in this parliament, that his party seems to have changed their attitude very greatly since the last session.
