From looking at some of the terms of the bill I think the hon. member will admit that a considerable amount of study will be required to determine just what would be the economic effects on shipping on the great lakes, on railroad operating crews, who doubtless will soon be going into negotiation, and who I believe as a matter of fact are in negotiation. Also hospitals and other services which are required to carry on a continuous operation are affected. Even the legislation that is provided in the province of Saskatchewan, to which I believe the hon. member referred, makes certain provisions

exempting the government from the requirement to pay two and a half times the base pay.
If I might read from a publication issued by the Department of Labour in December 1962 under the former minister, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), entitled "Provincial Labour Standards", there are two paragraphs here which are relevant. This is respecting legislation in the province of Saskatchewan:
If required to work on a holiday, employees in all work places except hotels, restaurants, hospitals, nursing homes and educational institutions must receive, in addition to their regular pay for the holiday, time and one half the regular rate for every hour or part of an hour worked, in effect, two and one half times their regular pay.
The key word there, of course, is "except". They are excepting hospitals, restaurants, hotels, nursing homes and educational institutions.
It is also to be noted that the legislation in this province, this great socialist utopia, does not go quite as far as is indicated in Bill No. C-2. Two and one half times the base rate is really not consistent with the purposes of the legislation. With all due respect to the hon. member, I would say that he has taken a more realistic attitude and has provided, in effect, for triple time, or three times the going rate. This, in my opinion, is more consistent, for after all the purpose of requiring punitive pay is in order to prevent where possible an employer working anyone on a statutory holiday. I recall negotiating perhaps the first agreement in the mining industry providing for pay for statutory holidays. I recall at that time the members of the committee seeming quite happy to accept time and a half for statutory holidays. This indeed is retrogressive. This does not do anything. It merely provides that an employer may continue to employ his workers and just as if it were a week end to pay no more than half a day's punitive pay. This having established the fact that payment will be made for no work, then accepting double time is, as I say, simply retrogressive. It means that any man can work on a statutory holiday and it costs nothing. There is no punishment or anything punitive about the legislation at all. So in order to be consistent triple time is the point at which we should arrive. As I said earlier, in 1947 Saskatchewan brought in this legislation but have done nothing about it since. They are still only given time and a half to an employee working on a statutory holiday so that it is not really a punitive measure.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make it clear that I think the principle of the bill is an excellent one and
474	HOUSE OF
Provision for Paid Statutory Holidays one with which I do not think any member on this side of the house would quarrel, in terms of the objective set forth. I am concerned about one or two aspects of the application of the bill which I think could bear closer examination, notably the type of employment to which it applies. There is no mention, for example, of employment in hospitals where certainly the federal government has a number of people who are very much concerned with continuous operation and are obliged to work on statutory holidays.
It seems to me that the question of the regulation of hours for certain categories of employment, and not only hours but statutory holidays, is a matter which in certain instances should be allowed to go to arbitration. As a member of this house I hope to be able to support legislation which will provide the right of compulsory arbitration on matters which are in dispute between the government as an employer and those associations that represent the employees of various crown corporations and the departments of the government service.
As I read and understand the bill, the problem here is that the application of section 4, for instance, in the case of hospital services where continuous operation is required would lead to unequal pay for particular periods for people doing the same work. If a person worked on a statutory holiday he would be paid at one rate. If by reason of the nature of the shifts he was obliged to work on a holiday he would get a premium in respect of that week. Therefore the pay cheques of different employees doing the same kind of work and working the same hours in that week would not be the same at the end of the week.
The appropriate machinery to rectify such a situation would be by negotiation with recognized employees associations, and by arbitration. I hope it will be possible to devise legislation that will give employees this right. This is certainly something which has been supported by members on this side of the house and I am firmly of the opinion that amendments to legislation governing the civil service generally and granting this right to employees would be a more effective and equitable means of dealing with the question of compensation for employees on shift work who work side by side and where one works on a statutory holiday and another does not with the result that at the end of the week their pay cheques are different in spite of the fact that they have performed substantially equivalent service at the same level of responsibility.
In this day and age I do not think anyone is prepared to say that we are going to be


so backward in employing people as to deny employees statutory holidays. The problem has been one of administrative interpretation and lack of uniformity of interpretation and it may well be that the appropriate answer will have to be found in legislation.
As a new member of the house this is the first piece of legislation on which I have had the privilege of speaking. Under the type of procedure to which 1 have been exposed there is an opportunity to bring forward, examine and possibly rectify questions of this nature within the scope of a regular procedure. I am in favour of such a process in this instance which would guarantee equity to everybody concerned. It seems to me that this is essential before we adopt legislation, because once it is adopted it is not easily changed.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That a special committee be appointed to consider matters relating to defence and to report from time to time its observations and opinions thereon; that the committee have power to send for persons.

papers and records and to examine witnesses; that it be empowered to adjourn from place to place; that standing order 67 be suspended in relation to the committee; and that the committee consist of 18 members to be designated by the house at a later date.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of satisfaction that I approach this debate concerning the establishment of a special defence committee. It is something for which I have asked a number of times during the last parliament, and I believe it is the answer to much of the confusion that presently exists, not only within this house but across the country in relation to what the actual defence needs of this country are. I should like, for a moment, to refer to remarks I made on January 24 when we were in the midst of the last defence debate. I referred the then prime minister to the fact that a defence committee could be the answer to the dilemma in which he found himself. I quote from Hansard of that date, page 3091;
The Prime Minister so far has refused to set up an all-party parliamentary committee on defence. We believe he is wrong in this refusal. It would be well for him to remember that this is a house of minorities and that neither he nor any of us knows which political party will be responsible for Canada's government and defence policy even three months from now. We ask that all parties together may have a chance to work out with proper information a constructive policy for our country in its relations with other nations of the world and in our own internal policy in which Canadians of every political allegiance can have confidence.
I believe that those words were true then, and they are just as true now. Therefore, we do give our wholehearted support to the setting up of a defence committee, with the hope that in the light of the remarks which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made this afternoon in relation to the committee's terms of reference there will be an opportunity to carry through to the real objectives of such a defence committee. This committee should be the means of assisting the government and assisting all of us in understanding what our defence policy should be.
The other day the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smallwood) stated he felt there was no need for minority parties. It might be an embarrassment, nevertheless, he must realize that some 25 per cent of the electors, or some two million voters during the last election turned to an alternative to the old line parties because the old parties have not faced up to their responsibilities in government.
In so far as this defence committee is concerned, I believe we have evidence that this has been a worth-while suggestion made by our party. Defence is too important a subject to be swept under the rug or to become the
30. 1963
Appointment of Defence Committee pawn of this political chess game. The lives of our people and the future of our country are involved. There is no doubt that the defence issue is, even at this time, a confused picture. Both the major parties have undergone a reversal of policy in connection with nuclear arms within the past few years. We have heard a great deal from the members of the official opposition about the reversal of policy which the Prime Minister has seen fit to make within the past year. This is well known. It was clearly stated over and over again during the last election campaign.
However, the Liberal party is not the only party that has reversed itself in the last couple of years. This is a fact that has become more or less obscured in the charges which have been levelled at the Prime Minister. I should like to refer to the issue of Hansard for February 20, 1959, where I find these words, at page 1223:
Under the irresistible dictates of geography the defence of North America has become a joint enterprise of both Canada and the United States. In the partnership each country has its own skills and resources to contribute, and the pooling of these resources for the most effective defence of our common interest is the essence of production sharing. Believing that parliament and the people of Canada are determined that this nation shall play its full part in terms both of quantity and quality in deterring and resisting aggression, the government intends that the Canadian forces will be well equipped and well trained for the Canadian share of these tasks in a balanced, collective defence.
In keeping with that determination careful thought is being given to the principles that in our opinion are applicable to the acquisition and control of nuclear weapons. The government's decisions of last autumn to acquire Bomarc missiles for air defence and Lacrosse missiles for the Canadian army were based on the best expert advice available on the need to strengthen Canada's air defence against the threat to this continent, and on its determination to continue an effective contribution to the NATO shield.
The full potential of these defensive weapons is achieved only when they are armed with nuclear warheads. The government is, therefore, examining with the United States government questions connected with the acquisition of nuclear warheads for Bomarc and other defensive weapons for use by the Canadian forces in Canada, and the storage of warheads in Canada. Problems connected with the arming of the Canadian brigade in Europe with short range nuclear weapons for NATO's defence tasks are also being studied.
We are confident that we shall be able to reach formal agreement with the United States on appropriate means to serve the common objective.
Those were the words of the leader of the official opposition. It has, then, become very evident that not only has the party with the responsibility of forming the government at this time changed its stand completely on defence, but so has the Conservative party.
It is not necessary at this time to go back and review the situation which led up to the cancellation of the Arrow. This was not just the cancellation of a project but was the

Appointment of Defence Committee actual sweeping out of an industry. Bomarc bases when installed cost some $700 million. We have just read that they are practically useless without nuclear warheads. Here was a decision to spend $700 million, and a moral commitment not only to the taxpayers of Canada but to the government and people of the United States. When we talk about there not being a commitment we are not facing up to actual facts, because certainly the fact that these bases were constructed and carriers were acquired points to a policy. In the developing picture of science and technology, including military equipment, there is nothing wrong with declaring a weapon to be obsolete if the facts are that it has been replaced with something more effective. However, we must be honest with the public and ourselves.
I believe that the confusion which has developed in regard to defence has come about through the inability and failure of our leaders in government to face up to the fact that some of these things are taking place. I have no objection, if what is being done is in the best interests of the nation in the light of the circumstances at the particular time it is done. In this situation, particularly here in parliament, nobody in the opposition can actually evaluate what a defence policy ought to be unless he is given the basic information and all the facts that are involved.
Therefore I think it is the responsibility of the government, which itself has the responsibility of forming policy and implementing it, to see that the opposition are at least informed of the facts and information which they must have if they are to judge the position with any intelligence at all.
Any defence policy which comes out of this parliament should have the confidence of every party in the house. Granted, it is the responsibility of the government to declare policy, but it is also the responsibility of Her Majesty's loyal opposition to know what that policy is, and second, why it has been adopted. That is why I think in a matter such as defence, which is vital to the well-being and the survival of our country, that the government face up to the responsibility of seeing not only that its members are informed in so far as possible, but also of seeing that the opposition have the facts which caused the policy to be stated in the first place, and then to know what the policy actually is.
We on this side of the house are pleased that the government has seen fit so quickly to bring in this resolution setting up the committee to deal with the thorny problems of defence. I maintain these problems cut across all party lines, and therefore the best way of seeking to solve our problems is to do it on a non-partisan basis. This is not

something new in other countries. It may seem strange and may be new to us here, but we should be able to learn objective lessons from others that can help us in the things we are actually dealing with now.
I am gratified that the minor parties are going to have fair representation on this committee, and therefore we were very pleased to support the enlargement of the committee from 18 to 24 members. I would again remind the government that the two smaller parties represent some 25 per cent of Canadian public opinion so far as voting strength is concerned, and that it is absolutely necessary to have this representation which is being allowed at present. This has made it possible for both smaller parties to have at least two members on the committee, something which is essential.
It was also heartening to hear the Prime Minister speak this afternoon and say that this defence committee will have the opportunity to discuss policy. This brings me to the point that I believe we should be carefully considering the terms of reference upon which the committee will base its work. If it is just another committee, as someone has said, to provide a means of getting away from responsibility, then that is not good enough. If it is a committee that actually goes to work and assists not only the government but all of us in our understanding of what the defence policies of our country should be, then we must outline the terms of reference.
I note that it will be possible for this committee to call witnesses regarding past and present events and future possibilities, that may have influenced what our policy should be today, and will influence what it might be tomorrow. Once more I say these terms of reference are essential, simply because parliament has a responsibility to itself in regard to defence matters.
As I listened to the Prime Minister this afternoon it seemed to me he was making a great thing about the fact that the committee will have the opportunity to discuss policy, but on the other hand, unless the terms of reference of the committee go further than that, then it will not be able to accomplish at least what I expect it can and should accomplish. Therefore I would suggest that the following points should be considered by the government, and also by the committee before it actually gets down to work. There may be other points involved, but as I think over the confused picture of our defence needs and what our defence policy should be, these points come to me as being the most important.
One is the anticipated pattern of potential aggression against Canada. We all agree that

we are not interested in any kind of offensive war, or even offensive weapons. We are interested in defending ourselves and at the same time carrying out our full share of responsibility in our struggle for the peace every Canadian looks for, and which I am sure we all agree is our responsibility to strive to achieve.
Second, what is the degree of subversion against Canada, and correlated with that what is the position of our security arrangements? This is something about which I am concerned. I recall that last February the Ottawa Citizen made mention of an information blackout which had been ordered by the government in 1960. I believe the former prime minister, former external affairs minister Green, and public works minister Fulton were involved in it. In this regard there must be as much classified information as possible made available to the committee. This means that it would have to be treated at times as confidential information, but it is the only manner that parties can be informed in an understanding way of the reasons why our defence needs are as they are.
Another point is, how far are peace and disarmament movements expressions of public opinion? We have a large number of peace and disarmament movements, all very vociferous in expressing their objection to the acquisition of any type of nuclear defence weapons, I am concerned, and I believe the public are as well, with the question whether or not some of these movements are legitimate, taking into regard the security of the nation.
Another point is, what forms of defence are practical within our physical ability and within our resource capability? We want to safeguard our country and carry out our responsibilities to our neighbours and friends, on this continent and throughout the western world, to the maximum degree of our ability but, Mr. Speaker, there are some things we can do well and there are some things which are more difficult for us to do. We agree we cannot have a defence policy of our own, entirely by ourselves. It can only be effective as we co-operate with our neighbours and our friends. I think the committee should be able to investigate this question very carefully. I would much sooner see our defence contribution worked out in such a way that we contributed to over-all projects instead of being just a splinter part of larger projects which are beyond us. I am sure the value of the surveillance of our skies, our waters and the radar surveillance of our northland is something that we understand as being within the reach of our capabilities. But trying to become a militaristic nation is something for which Canada does not have the resources and 28902-5-31
Appointment of Defence Committee for which I do not think we have an over-all obligation. If we can work out with our friends and neighbours where we can make the greatest contribution, I think we will get the best value for our defence dollar.
Another point is this. How far do foreign policies and trade policies relate to and tie in with our defence needs? I do not think it is possible any longer, particularly in the light of the cold war and the enemy which we face in it, to separate completely our trade policies and foreign policies from our defence policy. Our enemy does not work that way. These ideals, which have been passed on to us through our heritage, simply do not meet our needs today because the enemy that we face does not follow that kind of a code. Therefore I think this committee ought to be concerned with studying these matters and recommending back to parliament and the government the degree of co-ordination which should exist between foreign trade policy, external affairs policy and defence.
We hear a great deal about military defence and we speak about the department responsible for it as the department of defence. All the while we make it very clear both to ourselves and to the world that we are a country of peace. Canada has done a great deal tc further the cause of peace. On the other hand, I do not think we should ever take for granted that what we are doing is sufficient. I believe this defence committee should have within its terms of reference the authority to study and investigate every possible means of furthering peace and reaching the objective not only of nuclear disarmament on a multilateral basis but also of disarmament on a much wider scale than that. This is work that a committee can do.
There is an opportunity before us, in the setting up of this committee, to prove that there is a value to committees. To carry out some of the studies to which I have referred would mean that the committee would probably have to be divided into subcommittees, who would report back to the main committee on certain aspects where specialization and time is a prerequisite. That in itself would be good. But if we are to add to the collective knowledge which must be used to judge this tremendous problem of maintaining peace, and at the same time maintaining adequate defences for our country, we must broaden the base as far as we can. Therefore to object to such a committee being set up now is, I think, burying one's head in the sand in regard to the facts and procedures which should now be used by parliament. Let us not maintain the status quo just for the sake of maintaining the status quo, any more than we should criticize just for the sake of criticism.

Appointment of Defence Committee
We are told that the recent NATO council meeting which was held in Ottawa did not accomplish very much. I think the very quietness of this meeting was due to the fact that there is no crisis at this time. We may tend to prejudge the effectiveness of NATO simply because at this particular time there does not happen to be a world crisis facing us. But let us not let that condition fool us into thinking that we are at peace in this cold war and that things are coming our way. The cold war is just as real as it ever was, simply because our enemy in the cold war has promised that it will not stop until it destroys the very way of life which we regard as the only way that civilization can survive in the world. It is therefore very important that we take every precaution to make sure that our defences are adequate and that the policy we are using to provide these defences is the right one.
The cold war is not one of our choosing. We the Canadian people want nothing more than to live in peace, to live in peace with ourselves and our neighbours, having the objective of developing the human and material resources of the world. But we are at war with communism because communism is at war with us. We must be on guard to make sure we are aware of the dangers and are prepared to meet them, not after they have met us but before they reach us.
I am sure the people of Canada want to be informed to the extent that technical and classified information can be given to the public. We all want to do our part, however humble our situation, in making sure that peace is maintained. So it comes back to us in parliament to make sure that this defence committee does clear away the confusion that exists about defence. This is not a confusion only in the minds of we who are in parliament or the members of the public. Even the technical people themselves seem to be confused, because you often get one answer to a question from one person, and another answer to the same question from another person. This is illustrated by what we have all seen reported in the press.
We have maintained a policy since the end of world war II that the only way we can have peace and win the cold war is to contain the threat of communism. This policy has been right. Those who are critical of the necessity of spending money for defence and who question our defensive measures ought to remind themselves that probably if we had not had these defence policies since the end of world war II Europe, and who knows, maybe North America, would have been overrun by communism before now.
Public confidence has been shaken by this game of old party leapfrog regarding our


defence policy. Confidence will be restored when it is known that representatives of all parties have had the opportunity to inform themselves and understand the weighty and difficult problems which influence decisions on matters of defence policy. That is why, again, we are pleased this committee will be set up, and look forward with a great deal of expectation to seeing it play a constructive part in this over-all defence picture.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of supporting this motion to set up a special select committee relating to defence matters. I had hoped that the motion to set up this committee would be the occasion for a full-dress debate on the broad concepts of Canada's defence policy.
I must say I was disappointed that neither the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) nor the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) have made any statement to this house outlining in broad and general terms the policy which the government proposes to follow. Naturally, we do not expect them to give a detailed program at this time; that will be part of the functions of the committee. But before the house even met, ministers of the crown were constantly stating there would be an early opportunity for a full debate on defence matters. It is true that during the debate on the address there was a discussion of one narrow aspect of defence, that of nuclear arms in connection with the amendment I moved. However, the subject of national defence is a much broader question than the subject of nuclear arms. I still expect the Minister of National Defence to make a statement in the course of this debate in order that the country and the House of Commons may have a clear statement before them outlining the position the government takes with regard to defence matters. The minister of defence has never been a shrinking violet in talking about defence outside this house, and one would not expect him to be shy in this public forum.
We are supporting this motion because we believe a defence committee can serve a useful purpose. We believe it would have proved still more useful had it been set up before the government committed itself to a nuclear policy, rather than after the government has committed itself publicly to other countries and, apparently, to the ministerial council of NATO. It is difficult to evolve a non-partisan defence policy when a partisan defence policy has already been adopted in spite of the fact that there has been a division in this house on the question.
The value of the work which this committee can do will depend on whether it is permitted to deal with broad policies of

defence and international affairs, because these fields touch each other at so many points that they cannot be separated. It would be greatly preferable for the committee to discuss these larger aspects of the subject rather than that it should become immersed in technical details of military equipment and expenditure. I was glad to hear the Prime Minister say this afternoon that the terms of the motion, "all matters relating to defence", would include policy matters. Since I take it that the present motion constitutes the terms of reference of the committee, I trust that whoever is chairman of the committee will interpret the terms of reference as broadly as did the Prime Minister this afternoon. Certainly, as far as the New Democratic party members on that committee are concerned, they will insist that the committee's attention be primarily directed toward policy and Canada's role in the world defence situation.
I think everyone agrees that Canada needs a clearly defined defence policy which is consistent with her needs and in keeping with her economic resources. The Romans had a maxim: "If you wish for peace prepare for war". Captain Liddel Hart in his book "Defence or Deterrent" tears that argument to shreds and says: "If you wish for peace, understand war". When the Romans uttered their well-known maxim, what they really meant was that in times of peace one should prepare for victory. The world situation has changed tremendously since 1945 when the atomic era was ushered in. No country now can prepare for victory, because in a nuclear war there is no victory, only annihilation; and there can be no victor, only a nation which in the process of destroying its adversary would itself become a wasteland.
Canada has never had a clearly defined defence policy. We have had only a functional approach throughout our history. This is due to the fact that for many years we had a semi-colonial status and our defence policy was tied in with that of Great Britain. In the South African war our military forces became part of the British expeditionary force. In the first world war it was only with great difficulty that Sir Robert Borden and Sir Samuel Hughes managed to retain the identity of the Canadian corps. Even in the second world war, many of us will remember, the minister of defence for air, Mr. Chubby Powers, fought a long battle to keep the R.C.A.F. from being absorbed in the R.A.F. The reason we had a functional approach throughout this long period of our history was that Great Britain was one of the great military powers in the world, if not one of the greatest, and we sheltered behind the 28902-5-312
Appointment of Defence Committee protection of the British navy. But in the past few years two great military powers have emerged and the world has polarized around them. Canada must now enunciate a defence policy of her own in the light of this polarization. To use the words of James M. Minifie we now have the choice between becoming peacemaker or powder monkey. We have to decide whether we are to play an effective role in the world community or whether we are to become a military satellite of one of the great powers.
We in this group believe that Canada's defence role must of necessity be built around three centres, because there are three agencies with which we are now associated in matters of defence, namely, the United Nations, NATO and NORAD. What I assume this committee will be discussing is the order of priorities-where the emphasis should be laid. A defence policy, to have any merit in a changing world, must be a flexible policy so that the emphasis can change from year to year and from decade to decade.
The first agency to which I referred is the United Nations. In a world where nuclear war means disaster for all who participate, collective security on a world scale is the only answer. Regional pacts and military alliances should never be accepted as more than temporary expedients. The danger is that we shall come to rely too much upon regional defence pacts and resist the transfer of power to an international authority. If we are ever to build a world community based on the rule of law, there must be over the years this gradual transfer of authority and power from regional pacts to a world police force.
Clemenceau once said that war was too important to be trusted to generals. I submit it is indeed more true of peace. The great danger is that having built up military alliances we shall think solely in terms of military alliances because of those who have a built-in interest in maintaining those regional military alliances. It was a great soldier of the last war, president Eisenhower, who put this matter very succinctly in his farewell address to the American people in 1961. This is what he said:
We have been compelled to create a permanent armaments Industry of vast proportions. Added to this, three and one half million men and women are directly engaged in the defence establishment. We annually spend on military establishment security alone more than the net income of all United States corporations.
Then he went on:
In the councils of government we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex. The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist. We must never let the weight of this combination endanger our liberties or democratic processes. We

Appointment of Defence Committee
should take nothing for granted. Only an alert and knowledgeable citizenry can compel the proper meshing of the huge industrial military machinery of defence with our peaceful methods and goals so that security and liberty may prosper together.
I think that is a warning that all nations might well heed.
In his book "Juggernaut: The Warfare State", Fred J. Cook has pointed out that in 1961, in the United States, 100 top corporations alone got $21 billion of army procurement orders, with General Dynamics leading the field with $1,260 million; and that 86.4 per cent of all the army purchases were awarded without competitive bidding. The Herbert investigating committee in 1959-60 in the United States found that more than 1,400 retired officers from the rank of major, up, were employed by the top 100 corporations, including 261 generals or officers of flag rank. General Dynamics alone had 27 retired generals and admirals on its payroll.
We suggest that if this nation of ours and the other nations of the world are to move steadily toward the idea of collective world security, we must not allow those with a built-in interest in maintaining military alliances to prevent the evolution of a world police authority. It is in the United Nations that Canada can make its major contributions to the peace of the world. We can make it in many ways. We can make it by supplying conventional forces for policing action as we have already done on a small scale. Canada has the confidence of the Afro-Asian nations in a manner which is not enjoyed sometimes by other white nations. We have no territorial ambitions, we have no imperialistic designs, so oftentimes our forces can be used when other countries' forces are not acceptable. The fact that we are going to become a nuclear power may make us less acceptable, but certainly we have been acceptable in the past and we could be acceptable in the future.
Highly mobile mechanized Canadian conventional forces is one of the major contributions which Canada could make to a world police force. We could contribute through the United Nations by increasing supplies of food, raw materials and personnel with technical know-how to assist the undeveloped countries of the world. Mr. Speaker, we who are members of this house know very little about Canada's economic program. If one contrasts this with the United States, where a congressional committee examines every detail, in some cases visits the countries to look at the various projects which are undertaken by that very generous nation, we would see how little we know about what Canada is doing and how very little interest, in the
IMr. Douglas.]

main, Canadians take in this question. We would then begin to realize how much more of a contribution we could make.
The world has paid tribute to the great contribution which was made to the rehabilitation of Europe by the Marshall plan. Why not a Martin plan for Canada? Why not a bold and imaginative program for Canada? We are spending at the present time $60 or $70 million on economic aid. We could spend five or ten times this amount. This would, in the long run, make a greater contribution to peace than many of the purposes for which we have spent money on defence over the past 15 years.
The second agency around which a defence program must be built is NATO. The original purpose of NATO was to stop the spread of Russian armies across western Europe, and in this it has been successful. Tactical nuclear weapons were suggested for NATO largely because of the preponderant superiority of the Russians in the field of conventional weapons and manpower, and because the strategic deterrent, the intercontinental ballistic missile, was not at that time in a state of complete readiness.
The use of tactical nuclear weapons was based on the military theory of limited nuclear war. The interesting thing is that today most of the military thinkers who espoused this theory are now reversing their position. One of the greatest military thinkers in the United States, Henry A. Kissinger, who first advanced the idea of limited nuclear war has now called a halt. These are his words in making up a long article on this question:
In these terms the nuclear establishment on the continent is both dangerous and useless. It is dangerous because it may make inevitable the limited nuclear war both Mr. McNamara and Mr. Gilpatric have declared is certain to escalate. And it is useless because it will merely duplicate attacks on targets already covered by our strategic forces.
Mr. Gilpatric, the under secretary of state for defence in the United States, put it very clearly when he said:
I, for one, have never believed in a so-called limited nuclear war. I just don't know how you build a limit into it once you start using any kind of a nuclear bang.
The fact is that the real defence of the west today lies in the strategic nuclear deterrent in the form of intercontinental ballistic missiles. There can be no doubt that this deterrent has now reached staggering proportions. Dr. Lapp in his book, "Kill and Overkill", says that the United States now has sufficient nuclear capacity to destroy every person in the Soviet union ten times over and that the Soviet union has the nuclear capacity to destroy the United States five times over. It may well be that we have

reached the stage in world armaments of overkill, that we may have reached the stage where we must start to find some way of withdrawing rather than adding further to the great stockpile of nuclear weapons. Mr. McNamara, defence secretary of the United States, said before a congressional committee:
There is no question but today our strategic retaliatory forces of bombers, missiles and Polaris are fully capable of destroying Soviet targets even after absorbing an initial nuclear surprise attack.
It seems to me, therefore, a sad thing that Canada is contributing to the nuclear force at the very time when the whole trend of military thinking its toward conventional weapons. The weapons which we contribute to NATO cannot by any stretch of the imagination be called defence weapons. The Honest John artillery rocket has a explosive capacity of 60 kilotons, three times as powerful as the bomb that wiped out Hiroshima. This is hardly a defensive weapon. It was said the other day by Judge Thorson that the CF-104 Starfighters will carry a bomb with a one megaton explosive capacity. When the government was asked last Monday whether or not this was correct it was neither confirmed nor denied.
These Starfighters have a range of 1,000 miles. This does not mean a deterrent against the Soviet union. This means laying waste to the cities of East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Rumania and Bulgaria. This is hardly likely to fan the hopes of peace in central Europe when we talk about equipping the Starfighter with a weapon capable of wiping out any one of the great cities of Canada. We should remember moreover, that when we equip the Starfighter with nuclear weapons we will have to remove them from French soil because of the provision of the French government that they will not allow nuclear weapons on French soil unless they are solely under French control.
In spite of the genuflections by the ministerial council of NATO last week in the direction of peace I for one, and I think my feelings were shared by many people, had grave misgivings about the statements which emanated from that conference. There was constant repetition of "our adversary" as though we were already at war. We believe that the day must come when NATO will become a part of the United Nations police force, and if we do not work toward that end then we risk the danger of NATO becoming a focal point of a military alliance for promoting the military and territorial ambitions of a rejuvenated and remilitarized Germany.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that we cannot separate defence from diplomatic programs to relieve tensions. It is not enough
Appointment of Defence Committee to keep on building up armaments against an alleged adversary. Side by side with defensive programs there must go a diplomatic program to relieve the tensions and the causes that lead to war. Not much progress has been made, and I think not too much good will on either side has been shown, about finding a solution to the Berlin crisis and in bringing about military disengagement in Europe.
May I say a word now about the third agency, NORAD. Under this agreement Canada was to join with the United States in continental defence. We were to accept Bomarc missile bases and to supply CF-101 or Voodoo planes, and this was for the purpose of repelling an attack by manned bombers. But today even Mr. McNamara, the defence secretary of the United States, says that the Bomarcs are losing their military value. He told a congressional committee that if it were not for the fact that it cost only some $20 million a year to maintain them he would suggest scrapping them.
Today the situation has entirely changed from what it was when NORAD was set up. The real threat today is from intercontinental ballistic missiles and against these there is no known defence at the present time except a counter-attack by other I.C.B.M.'s to knock out the opponent's missile bases. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I wonder whether this is not the real reason why we are being pressed so hard to accept nuclear weapons on Canadian soil. Certainly this seems to be the view expressed by General Simonds, who was chief of staff of the Canadian corps in 1941 and who had a distinguished military record in the last war. I quote now from the Toronto Star of February 20 where it says:
General Guy Simonds, former Canadian army chief of staff, suspects that the main reason the United States is "pressuring" Canada to accept nuclear warheads for its Bomarcs is to establish the principle that the U.S. may establish nuclear bases on Canadian soil.
"That is the only explanation that makes any sense," he said in an interview. "Even when Canada was making the decision to accept the Bomarc in 1959 military men in the U.S. were saying it was useless as a defensive weapon. Our poor little Bomarc bases couldn't knock out more than .0001 per cent of an attacking force. They will not defend Canada. They will not defend America, they do not make the slightest bit of difference in the present world balance of power."
Then he goes on to give what he thinks is the real reason for this pressure. He says:
"Within six months of the time Canada agrees to accept nuclear warheads for the Bomarc, I am convinced the United States will declare it obsolete and recommend another nuclear weapon. And by accepting nuclear warheads for the Bomarc we will have established the principle that will make it virtually impossible to turn down later proposals of a similar nature, no matter how much against our national interest they may be."

I hope this committee will call General Simonds and some of the other military experts in this country because I have the uneasy suspicion that the Bomarcs are not the issue at all; that eventually we shall be asked to station intercontinental ballistic missiles in Canada on the theory that the only way we can defend this continent is to have the capacity to knock out missile bases in the Soviet union in Siberia or in some other part of the world.
There is a growing uneasiness across this country as to why Canada at this time, when almost everyone from the President of the United States, down, is speaking of the growing importance of conventional weapons, at a time when there is no longer any inferiority of the west as compared to the east with regard to nuclear capacity, should acquire nuclear arms both under NORAD and under NATO. No explanation has been forthcoming for this complete about-face on the part of the government. One need only go back to November 14, 1961, at which time everyone saw the printed letter which the Prime Minister sent to the voice of women organization. In this letter, he said:
I was very glad of the opportunity to receive the delegations from the voice of women and the Canadian campaign for nuclear disarmament when they were in Ottawa last week. As I mentioned to them, I have always maintained that the nuclear powers should not be expanded and that Canadians should not accept nuclear weapons under either national control or jointly with the United States.
This is signed, "Yours sincerely, L. B. Pearson". This statement is less than six months old. This is why there is an uneasy feeling that we have not been told all the facts; that there is some reason for this complete about-face. One of my colleagues has already made reference to a book that was published last year entitled, "The Liberal Party" and written by one J. W. Pickersgill, who has very kindly autographed this copy for me. I might say that I bought it at a newsstand. It is one of the best investments I ever made. I think it will become more valuable as the years go by and as more and more promises fail to materialize. At page 133, the writer of this book says:
We do not believe, however, that it would strengthen the nuclear deterrent to equip the Canadian forces with nuclear weapons under national control. We hold this opinion, not on moral grounds but because we do not believe that Canada, by becoming a nuclear power itself, should provide any other country with an excuse to equip itself or its satellites with nuclear weapons, thereby increasing the number of nuclear powers.
I draw attention to the last phrase, "-thereby increasing the number of nuclear powers". At that time the writer thought that the acquiring of nuclear weapons made one a nuclear power. There was none of this hairsplitting chauvinism to the effect that you


have not become a nuclear power, you have not joined the nuclear club, until you have become an independent nuclear nation. There was no suggestion of that then.
The writer goes on as follows:
Moreover, it is quite clear that the Canadian forces will never have nuclear weapons under exclusively Canadian control, unless Canada manufactures her own weapons which we cannot afford and do not desire to do. The Liberal party believes that Canada can make a more appropriate and effective contribution to the joint defence of this continent and to the military alliance of the free world by strengthening the so-called conventional armaments of the Canadian forces than by seeking to become a very junior nuclear power, with a limited supply of nuclear weapons which, in present circumstances, could not be under Canadian custody.
The only reason we have been given for this complete political somersault in the course of a few short weeks is that there was a commitment made by the previous government. I do not know of any better reply to that than the one which appeared the other day in the Toronto Daily Star, a well known Liberal newspaper, not one of the new acquisitions of the Liberal party but one that has been traditionally with the Liberal party. This editorial is dated Tuesday, May 28, 1963 and reads as follows:
The Pearson government misleads the public when it claims it is accepting nuclear warheads only because of a "commitment" made by the former Diefenbaker administration.
The Liberals fostered this myth during the election campaign, despite repeated denials from former Prime Minister Diefenbaker. Yet External Affairs Minister Paul Martin still implies that it is the Conservatives, not the Liberals, who are responsible for Canada becoming a nuclear power.
"This government," he told the Commons last night, "has merely acted in respect of a commitment which was made by (the Diefenbaker) government."
Mr. Martin's bland explanation is unconvincing. If Canada is now committed to accept nuclear arms, it is because of a commitment made by Prime Minister Pearson, no one else.
Since taking office April 22, the Liberals have been challenged repeatedly to produce evidence that the former Conservative administration committed Canada to accept nuclear warheads. They have been able to produce none.
Indeed, even if the Conservatives had made such a commitment, the Liberal attitude raises a more fundamental question:
When a new government takes office, should it feel obliged to maintain the policies or "commitment" undertaken by its predecessor?
In our view, it should not. For what real progress could we expect at Ottawa if a government felt itself bound by the policies of a previous regime? A new administration cannot place itself in a position where it is a prisoner of policies which are no longer valid or which may have been discredited by the electorate at the polls.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say that the public is concerned, and that we in this party are concerned. We trust that this committee which will be set up as a result of the passing of this motion will be directed to

look at the defence policies of Canada, whether she should have a nuclear role and therefore a position of being a military satellite, or whether we can occupy the role of being a peacemaker in the world of nations and make our contribution to the establishment of the rule of law.

I speak with some conviction on this matter. I know that a committee of this kind has been resisted in the past by previous ministers of national defence but, notwithstanding that historical position, I came to the conclusion, two or three years ago, that with the technological changes that had taken place in the past ten years in particular, the subject of national defence was much too complicated and too complex just for a superficial examination. I felt that, in order to have an intelligent discussion in the House of Commons, and through the House of Commons, in the press of the country, a great deal more information would have to be made available, and a much more detailed examination of the facts would have to take place by a committee especially set up to spend a lot of time and energy on the study of that information.

speechtext: Answer the question. I know the answer. You give the answer.

I do not think you do, because in the two visits which you made to the department when you were the minister I do not think you had a chance to get all the

Appointment of Defence Committee background information. You were more concerned with other things. I hope you will not press me into indicating what they were.
Hear, hear.

I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend is aware that to use equipment as complicated and as expensive as the Honest John for an ordinary high explosive charge would not make any sense whatsoever, and it would be just about the clearest demonstration of futility in relation to resource input and output that could be imagined. In respect of the F-104, the particular version that we have, as I am sure my hon. friend is aware, and my colleagues and I attempted to warn him at the time the aircraft was chosen, is a very sophisticated aircraft. It is not a good all-purpose, general weapons platform, and the particular configuration purchased by this government was designed in such a way that it is virtually useless for anything except the role that was undertaken by the previous government; and the modifications which could make it useful for some other purpose are so considerable, and the effectiveness that it would have under those circumstances-
Like the Arrow.
-would be so low that no military adviser would ever recommend it to any government, I can assure you.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: A very unsatisfactory answer.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder
whether the minister would answer another question? Does he now consider that the Star-fighter, as he anticipates its use, will be effective?
Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the fact that it is a very sophisticated aircraft, I think it would be quite effective for the role for which the previous government acquired it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: One further supplementary question: I wonder if the hon. gentleman recalls the day when, asserting Liberal defence policy, he said the government should scrap plans to acquire the Starfighter and that no nuclear weapons should be used either on it or on Canadian soil.
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I think the government would have been well advised to have taken my advice at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the minister saw fit to make some comments, though I deplore the fact that he did not make what I thought he should have made, namely a first statement


as to government intentions and government policy. To my thinking-and to this extent I agree with the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas)-we shall obtain the maximum value from this committee only after there has been a confrontation between the government and the opposition-after there has been a joining of issues as to the facts upon which there may be a divergence of opinion. If this were done, I think the committee in proceeding with its work would have the necessary guide lines to enable it to carry out its task most effectively.
After listening to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) I am afraid it is all too easy to see that the committee may become bogged down in an avalanche of studies all more or less relevant to its task. The hon. member suggested a wide variety of subject matter which might well be discussed during the course of the committee's deliberations. A number of these suggestions were, it is true, relevant to the terms of reference; but bearing in mind the broad manner in which those terms of reference have been conceived and the different interpretations which have been placed on them by hon, members I find it difficult to see how the committee can accomplish anything useful except possibly over a long period of time. It may even have occurred to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that the members of this committee might ultimately be appointed to the other place where, in the more leisurely atmosphere which prevails, they might be able to come to some conclusion over a period of several years. Nevertheless, the committee could achieve something of value provided that at some time before this debate is concluded a spokesman on the government side sees fit to make a statement such as I suggested at the beginning of my remarks.
I wish, now, to speak briefly about one matter which has already provided scope for controversy tonight and which might well form the basis of considerable discussion in the committee, namely the question whether or not there was a commitment by the previous government with regard to the acquisition of nuclear arms. The Prime Minister and other members of the government have referred to what they consider as being adequate evidence to establish their view on this matter. I do not share their opinion. It has been suggested that General Norstad, who came to Canada at the turn of the year, made statements from which there is an inference to be drawn. It is interesting to read in a recent press comment that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) had some conversation with General Norstad short!v Kefore he came here. It would be

interesting to know-and possibly this information could be obtained during the committee hearings-whether General Norstad came here at the invitation of the Minister of National Defence and whether there was any prompting from the minister as to what he should say when he came here.
The Prime Minister suggested that the NATO communique issued by the 15 nations in 1957 after their deliberations forms the basis for what he suggests to be a contractual obligation by the Canadian government to take nuclear arms. I think it will be well to take a look at this particular document. It was cited by the Prime Minister, who read part of it, and it is to be found recorded at page 63 of Hansard of this year. I would particularly refer the house to the second paragraph of the communique, the part which was quoted by the Prime Minister:
The deployment of these stocks and missiles-
This refers to nuclear stocks and missiles. -and arrangements for their use will accordingly be decided in conformity with NATO defence plans and in agreement with the states directly concerned.
My submission is this: there are two essential requirements before there is an obligation or a contractual commitment. The signing of the communique does not in itself constitute such an agreement. I think a good point was made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam when he referred to Norway and Denmark, two nations belonging to the NATO organization, nations which had subscribed to this communique but which did not see fit to take nuclear weapons. I think the reason for this is plain. Until any one of those 15 nations which signed the communique enters into the agreement referred to in the second paragraph there is no binding obligation. The minister made some reference to this this evening. I am not in a position to know the length of time which would be required to conclude such an agreement, but there is no doubt about the terms of the United States atomic energy act-and, of course, we must consider ourselves in relation to the United States, the country from which the nuclear missiles would be obtained. Until an agreement has been reached, we are not bound. Neither is the United States bound. The United States, as conditions now exist, is under no commitment to furnish us with nuclear weapons. Not only is there no commitment but it would be a breach of the McMahon act if weapons were supplied.
As I understand the law of contract, there must be two parties to an agreement and until an agreement has been signed, there is no binding commitment and no obligation upon the government of Canada. As a matter 28902-5-321
Appointment of Defence Committee of fact, the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence for some time have been in possession of what they consider to be adequate information regarding the alleged commitment-and I underline the word "alleged".
In 1960 the present Prime Minister, speaking in an external affairs debate, made this categorical statement, as reported on page 985 of Hansard:
I think we had a right to conclude from that-
-the word "that" had reference back to a statement that the government had taken weapons which could be used with nuclear missiles-
-that the government had made a decision to use nuclear warheads on the Canadian weapons. If it means anything, it means that.
So the Prime Minister and his party are in this position, that they have indicated that as from February 11, 1960 in their opinion the Canadian government was obligated to take nuclear arms and that there was a firm commitment.
We heard nothing at that time of the sacred necessity of fulfilling our obligations. We heard nothing of the fact that Canadian prestige would suffer seriously and that our position would deteriorate if we did not fulfil these commitments. The so-called pledge was not of great concern to the Prime Minister and those of his party who were interested in this matter. I just point that out, and in support of this view I would put on the record these quotations from the speeches made by the Prime Minister and the present Minister of National Defence. The Prime Minister said on August 5, 1960, as reported on page 7606 of Hansard:
So far as continental defence is concerned-I start with that first-I repeat what my hon. friend said. In my view we should get out of the whole SAGE-Bomarc operation, and we should not spend any more money on radar gap fillers. Our objection to the Bomarc is not only that we do not think it is an effective weapon. I admit that, its tests lately have been certainly far more successful than the previous tests. Perhaps for certain purposes it may become an effective weapon, I do not know; but that is not our major objection to it. Our objection is to the kind of defence strategy it represents and which we do not think will be effective however effective the weapon may be.
Then follow these words:
If the United States wishes to continue that kind of protection, let the United States do so. Let us withdraw from that direct form of continental defence.
There is not one word about honouring commitments there, Mr. Speaker.
Then the Prime Minister said in the same debate, as reported on page 7605 of Hansard:
It is on that basis, on those principles-I would like to call them that-that I have tried to work

Appointment of Defence Committee
out my own views as to what our defence policy should be at this time. I admit at once that it is not easy to do that, and it has taken two or three years of what has been referred to in another context as agonizing reappraisal-
I might just say, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal party must have been in a perpetual state of agony since then, having in mind the frequent changes they have made. The Prime Minister went on:
-and I do not put them forward as anything final and fixed that could not be changed. They may even have to be changed-
Then later on he said:
After all, this kind of defence is primarily a United States responsibility. It is the defence of the deterrent. We know how important that is; but it is a deterrent which is under the sole control of the United States of America. It is not a defence, and in the nature of things I submit cannot be a defence, of our territory in the traditional sense of the word, and it will soon be no defence of anything. As the minister himself has indicated, in a few years missile attack will make this kind of defence of very minimal importance indeed, once missiles supersede airborne bombers, and that will not be long from now.
Then the Minister of National Defence said in 1961, as reported on page 8230 of Hansard for September 12:
It is interesting to note that in the long list of priority items presented by President Kennedy to congress on March 28 last there did not appear one of the major items on which the Canadian government is relying. Not one American penny for the Voodoo, the F-104, the Bomarc or the Honest John. The Canadian defence department has become a pawnshop for second hand American hardware.
Our position in this respect is the same as we announced last year. We still feel that atomic weapons in Canada are unnecessary at this time. We feel they are redundant. We do not think they add anything to the security of Canada, and we think they provide no protection for the strategic air command.
-if the Russians were to start a war now-
-and this is 1961, Mr. Speaker-

if they were to embark upon a direct attack, they would not do so unless they had enough missiles to cover every American strategic air command base on the north American continent. That is fundamental.
There is not one word there about commitments.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

If you do not mind, I have some more interesting comments to make. The hon. member might wish to amplify his question when I have finished.
The Prime Minister, as reported on page 8348 of Hansard for September 14, 1961, said:
Even if this Bomarc missile is effective-and we do not think it is effective; we think it is obsolete, and that the United States will soon be dropping it-
Defence of this kind, Mr. Chairman, is not going to save us, and Canadian participation in defence

of this kind is not going to be the best way in which we can discharge our obligations.
Mr. Speaker, there are some more remarks made by the Minister of National Defence, with whom I had the pleasure of appearing as a member of the special committee on defence expenditures in 1960, to which I should like to draw attention. At page 399 of the minutes of that committee meeting he had this to say:
The Bomarc is useless even with the nuclear warheads.
Later on the hon. gentleman, I must say with some reluctance, seconded a motion made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) that funds appropriated for the Bomarc should be removed from the year's expenditures.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? In face of that advice, why did the government which the hon. gentleman supported go ahead with the acquisition of the Bomarc?

In face of that statement, I would ask why did the minister go ahead with his program to get warheads for the Bomarc at this time?
Then speaking in support of the motion which he seconded he had this to say, as reported on page 491 of the minutes:
This is exactly the reason which has been given by the Liberal party for opposing the Bomarc installations. In the event of such an all out attack it would be an obvious thing for the Russians to set as their first targets as they approached the American continent by air with a missile attack, the Bomarc fixed installations and it would not be reasonable to expect these fixed installations to survive an initial attack. Therefore the defence provided by them and the return effect is nil.
Then later on he said:
As far as Canadian air defence is concerned, or as far as its contribution to the defence of the United States is concerned, in the event of an allout attack, such as was hypothecated by the parliamentary secretary, the Bomarc missile would offer no possibility of any defensive action.
There are one or two more positive rather than negative examples of this particular controversy as to whether or not commitments were made. I think it is fair to say that during the course of the whole of the hearings held by the defence expenditures committee, those at which I was present at least and I have read the proceedings fairly carefully, the then minister of national defence made it categorically plain that the Bomarc could be equipped with either a nuclear or conventional warhead. He did not budge one iota from that position which he established with his first statement.
On the same aspect, Mr. Speaker, I might also refer to a statement made by the present

Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), then the prime minister, when dealing with the agreement under which the Canadian authorities took the Voodoo aircraft as part of their obligation. He made this statement which appears at page 6179 of Hansard, June 12, 1961:
Canada will assume responsibilities hitherto resting on the United States ... for manning, operation, maintenance and financing 16 stations of this line.
That is the D.E.W. line.
Canada will be furnished with 66 F-101B interceptor aircraft and appropriate support equipment. These aircraft.. . will be armed with conventional weapons-
Those are the Voodoo aircraft. This was the statement in which the then prime minister advised the house and the country as to the terms under which these weapons were acquired and the equipment that came with them.
May I ask a question on that point?

I am about ready to sit down and I will have ample time then to answer the hon. member's question. I would just say that the discussions and deliberations of this committee could be well directed to that one point alone, whether or not any commitment was made by the previous government or whether or not the present government has used this an an obvious excuse in order that it might implement what I and millions of other Canadians think is the part of the terms of surrender negotiated in the treaty of Hyannis Port.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I understand the hon. member for Leeds has a question?

Yes. The hon. member has just concluded his remarks by referring to something the former prime minister said which indicated there was no nuclear commitment. I should like to read him one sentence from page 3136 of Hansard, January 25, 1963:
Following SACEUR's recommendation, as we saw the situation in 1959 and as I said earlier in my remarks, we undertook to equip our squadrons assigned to NATO for a strike reconnaissance role, which role would include the mission of delivering nuclear weapons. No one was under any misunderstanding in that connection. Parliament approved this program and appropriated the funds.
Does the hon. member not regard these remarks by the Prime Minister on January 25, 1963, as evidence of the assumption of a nuclear role for the CF-104 in NATO?
Appointment of Defence Committee
I do not regard them any more as a commitment than I regard what the hon. member has said as a question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Sherbrooke.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member would permit me one second to see whether it might be the wish of the house to go on a bit later this evening with a view to finishing this debate-
No.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -so that the committee could be set up and we could get on with other urgent business.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A suggestion has been made by the minister. Is there unanimous consent?
No.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a most important subject and there are other members of the house who would like to speak. I hope the house leader is not trying to limit debate on this matter.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, I can assure hon. members that nothing is further from my mind.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My thought was that in conformity with the suggestion made by his right hon. leader at the beginning of the session we might sit a little longer tonight so that hon. members who wish to speak could make their speeches while the other speeches are fresh in their mind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
A suggestion has been made which requires unanimous consent. This has not been given. Therefore I recognize the hon. member for Sherbrooke.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, may I point out that it is ten o'clock? (Text):

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed that we call it ten o'clock?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I really feel, sir, that we should sit at least until ten o'clock.
(Translation) :

Mr. Speaker, it was most agreeable to have the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) condescend to address this house. We had almost drawn the conclusion that his new office did not involve the responsibility of submitting from time to time a report of his activity to the House of Commons.
We could almost have believed that he had been gagged by exterior pressure.

Appointment of Defence Committee It was a pleasure to hear his voice, but I thought that under such important circumstances, he should not have dwelt at length on the theme of his last election campaign but that he should rather have explained the program he intends to put into effect, or the steps he intends to take in order that the defence committee may operate within its foreseen province.
I was also most unhappily surprised to hear other speakers, for instance the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), talking about an entirely different matter than that they should have commented upon. We were expecting suggestions about the defence committee but the hon. member simply stated his party's nuclear policy.
Then a Conservative member took pains to excuse the mistakes of the previous administration.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I take it that we are going on with interim supply tomorrow?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. Tomorrow we will take interim supply and then resume this debate. If this debate should be concluded we will take the first stage of the economic council measure. I would imagine that perhaps that would be all it would be possible to get done tomorrow.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, May 31, 1963
